prompt: next tuesday at 9 i get 20 minutes in the ops leadership meeting (room 3B, about 8 people) to get sign-off on moving the night shift from five 8-hour nights to four 10-hour nights. Maria Okafor, the COO, is the one who signs off. the two site managers, Tom Reyes and Jess Kowal, are against it because they think it'll wreck shift handovers, and they've both said so in email. Ana from HR is coming to check the legal side (overtime rules, rest periods). what's my running order and what do i actually say in the first two minutes?
rubric: The running order is built around getting a decision from the COO, with the specific decision asked for stated clearly and early, and a closing ask she can say yes or no to.
The site managers' handover objection is named and answered openly, in fairness to them, before the plan is presented as settled, rather than ignored or saved for questions.
HR's legal question gets its own short, explicit place in the order instead of being left to come up by chance.
The opening two minutes are written out as words to say and start from the room's concern or the decision, not a bio, a thank-you or an agenda read-out.
The plan fits a 20-minute slot, leaves time for discussion, and invents no data (no made-up productivity or cost figures presented as facts).

prompt: I'm presenting the postmortem for last month's checkout outage (2 hours 40 minutes down on a Saturday) at the all-engineering meeting on Thursday, about 120 engineers in the big room plus three execs: the CEO, the CFO and the VP of product. I have 25 minutes. The engineers will want the timeline and the root cause (a config change to the payment service's connection pool). The execs want to know if it'll happen again and what it costs to stop it. The fix we're proposing needs two engineers for one quarter. Outline it slide by slide.
rubric: Gives a slide-by-slide outline with a sensible number of slides for 25 minutes, with rough timings or an order that clearly fits the slot.
Early on, states in plain terms what happened, the impact, and whether it can happen again, so the execs are oriented before the technical detail.
The timeline and root cause have a clear place with enough depth for engineers, but are framed so a non-engineer can follow why it matters.
Ends on the decision being asked for and its cost (two engineers for a quarter), not on a generic thanks or lessons-learned list.
Does not invent figures such as revenue lost or incident counts; where numbers would help, it says they need to be supplied.

prompt: our lab spent three years testing six coating formulations for marine sensors (codes C1 to C6). C2 and C5 worked: under 5% signal drift after 18 months in seawater. C4 sort of worked (good drift but it peels at temperature swings). C1, C3 and C6 failed. i had a 20-minute slot at the industry consortium meeting and the organiser just cut everyone to 12 minutes. most of the 80 or so people there are buyers and procurement people from sensor makers, not chemists. i have 41 slides from our internal review. help me decide what goes in and what doesn't.
rubric: Makes a clear choice of what stays and what goes, centred on what buyers need to decide (which coatings to consider and under what conditions), rather than trimming each section evenly.
The two working coatings get most of the time; the failures are grouped briefly instead of each formulation getting equal treatment.
C4's limitation is kept in a form a buyer can act on, rather than dropped or buried.
Suggests telling the room openly what was left out and where to get it (a handout, report or follow-up), rather than cramming it in.
Gives a slide count or time budget that fits 12 minutes, well below 41 slides, and explains which chemistry detail to cut for this audience.

prompt: quick one: 5-minute update at my team's standup on friday about the new on-call rota. they asked for it and nobody's against it. facts: starts monday march 3; weekly shifts instead of daily; handover is mondays at 10am; 7 people in the rotation; swaps go in the shared calendar and need a 48h heads-up. just give me the slides.
rubric: Short: a small number of slides (roughly two to four) suitable for a 5-minute update to a friendly team.
The change and the start date (Monday March 3) appear up front, not after background or context slides.
Uses only the given facts (weekly shifts, Monday 10am handover, 7 people, 48h swap notice in the shared calendar) and invents no extra policies, names or numbers.
Does not add stakeholder analysis, objection handling, persuasion structure or a long preamble that the request did not need.
Slide text is plain and scannable, and it is easy to tell what each person must do.

prompt: Draft the slide titles and what goes on each slide. I'm proposing we replace our in-house search service with a hosted vendor. The four engineers who built the in-house one will be in the room, and so will my director, Priya Shah, who decides. 15 minutes, in her Wednesday staff meeting. My notes: in-house p95 latency 420 ms; vendor trial 180 ms on the same queries; the in-house service takes about 2.5 engineers' time a year to maintain; vendor quote $96k a year; one enterprise customer complained twice last quarter about search results; my best argument so far is that it's like renting versus owning a house.
rubric: Uses only the facts in the notes; no invented engineer salaries, migration timelines, vendor features or extra customer complaints stated as fact.
Puts the cost comparison on a common basis (2.5 engineers' time per year against $96k per year), and says the engineer cost needs a figure from the team rather than making one up.
Does not rest the case on the renting-versus-owning analogy or on the single customer's complaints; at most uses them as illustration, with the latency and maintenance numbers carrying the argument.
Treats the team that built the in-house service fairly: credits what it does, and does not frame the proposal as a verdict on their work.
Slide titles state the point of each slide, and the deck ends with the decision asked of the director.

prompt: I think the churn spike is mostly from the new onboarding emails, but I can't prove it yet. Facts: monthly churn went from 3.1% to 4.4% in the three weeks since the new emails went out on the 2nd; nothing else shipped in that window as far as I know; the March annual signups cohort churned less after the change (1.2% vs 1.6% before), which doesn't fit. I have 10 minutes with Leo Grant, the VP of growth, tomorrow at 2 in his office. What should the slides say?
rubric: Clearly separates what the data shows (the churn rise and its timing) from what is suspected (that the emails caused it).
Shows the March annual cohort result openly as evidence that does not fit, rather than hiding it or explaining it away.
The request to the VP is sized to the evidence, such as a test, rollback on a segment, or more weeks of data, not a confident call to scrap the emails.
Uses only the given numbers and does not invent extra cohorts, revenue impact or causes.
Fits 10 minutes: a few slides with titles that say the point, leading with the finding and the ask.

prompt: The client's template puts a progress bar with every section name across the top of each slide, and they insist we keep it. My 7 slide titles for a 15-minute supplier review with their procurement team next Monday: Agenda; Q3 delivery performance; Late shipments root causes; Quality incidents; Cost changes; Proposed fixes; Next steps. Make them work inside their template.
rubric: Keeps the client's progress bar as required and does not argue for removing it or redesigning the template.
Rewrites the titles so each one states what the slide says (a finding or claim) rather than only naming a topic, while the bar keeps the section names.
Does not invent specific figures in the new titles; uses placeholders or asks for the numbers where a title needs one.
Handles the Agenda slide sensibly given the bar already shows the sections (for example drops it or turns it into a one-line summary), with a short reason.
Keeps the scope to the titles and their fit with the template, without a full restructure of the review the user did not ask for.

prompt: presenting quarterly NPS on a zoom call this thursday to about 60 people across sales and support, most cameras off. I have one line chart: 8 quarters x 4 regions (NA, EMEA, LATAM, APAC). the point is that APAC dropped two quarters in a row (from 41 to 33) while the rest held roughly flat. how do i walk them through it?
rubric: Gives a concrete step-by-step order for walking through the chart: what the axes and lines are, then the regions that held, then the APAC drop.
Makes the APAC drop the clear focus, for example by highlighting APAC and greying the other lines or building the chart up in stages.
Accounts for a remote audience with cameras off: says where to look in words, avoids relying on pointing, and checks in or pauses since the speaker cannot read the room.
Suggests a slide title or spoken line that states the point (APAC down two quarters in a row) rather than a generic 'NPS by region'.
Does not invent reasons for the APAC drop; if causes are mentioned, they are framed as things to find out or bring.

prompt: I'm giving the opening keynote at a logistics conference in Denver next month, 30 minutes, about 400 people. Around minute 12 I tell a two-minute story about the night our Columbus warehouse flooded and the night crew moved 3,000 orders to the other site by hand. The point of the talk is that the plans that work are the ones the front line can change without asking. What should be on screen while I tell the story, and what slide comes right after?
rubric: Makes a specific choice for the screen during the story (for example a black or near-blank slide, or one photo of the flooded floor) and explains why it suits a story told live.
Advises against putting the story's text or bullet points on screen while it is being told.
The slide right after the story turns it into the talk's point (front-line people changing the plan without asking), stated plainly rather than left for the audience to infer.
Ties the story to the talk's main idea, not as a stand-alone anecdote, and keeps it close to two minutes.
Stays within what the user said happened and does not invent details of the flood as facts.

prompt: I'm recording a 6-minute video walkthrough of our Q3 results that the 200 or so people in the company will watch on their own time, mostly on laptops, after it's posted on the intranet. There's no live session. I want a short customer story in the middle and a minute explaining why gross margin fell. Where should I put pauses for stories or explanation, and what's on screen during them?
rubric: Keeps something meaningful on screen during the story and the explanation (for example a supporting photo, a quote, or the margin chart with the relevant part highlighted), rather than a blank or black slide.
Treats the viewer as self-paced: on-screen text can carry a little more since people can pause, but still does not duplicate the voiceover word for word.
Places the story and the margin explanation at sensible points in the 6 minutes, with each section's point visible on screen as a title or caption.
Does not apply live-room advice that does not fit a recording, such as reading the room, taking questions, or pausing for audience reaction.
Does not invent the Q3 figures or the customer story's details.
